extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in propaganda, media studies, and political/psychological operations
extracted.subtask_description: Describing and categorizing historical and modern propaganda methods, targets, and effects across conflicts and societies; identifies tactics used by states, insurgents, and non-state actors and points of vulnerability (e.g., children, domestic audiences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda as part of a Strategic Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda used systematically by political leadership as part of a broader Strategic Plan to achieve territorial, demographic, or political objectives (e.g., link populated areas, gain control, create a sovereign entity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page explains that in the Bosnian war ICTY verdicts found propaganda was part of the Serb Strategic Plan to link Serb-populated areas and remove non-Serbs; the leadership was aware the plan would require force and war crimes, and propaganda was used to justify/prepare those actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seizure and control of local media and public institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking over television/radio stations and public institutions to establish direct channels for nationalist or partisan messaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Croat forces seized broadcasting stations (e.g., Skradno), created local radio/TV to carry propaganda, raised flags over public buildings, and imposed currency—used to signal control and intimidate/force population changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media justification, revision, and denial of mass crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Using media to justify, revise, or deny mass war crimes committed by one's own forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serb media made efforts to justify or deny mass war crimes; Croatian journalists testified as defence witnesses attempting to relativise crimes. This tactic aims to shape narratives, absolve perpetrators, and undermine victims' accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinated use of national and local media outlets and influential journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobilizing both local stations and national newspapers/TV and leveraging prominent reporters to amplify partisan narratives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Croatian Radiotelevision and newspapers like Večernji list supported local propaganda; named journalists (e.g., Dijana Čuljak) are cited as amplifiers and sometimes accused of incitement. Guidance: coordinate outlets and personalities to lend credibility and reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological operations (PSYOP) – jamming and replacement broadcasting
rubrics_metrics.description: Jamming enemy/local broadcasts and transmitting replacement messages using dedicated platforms (e.g., aircraft) to demoralize opponents and win local sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Afghanistan EC-130E Commando Solo aircraft jammed local radio and transmitted replacement propaganda. This includes technical measures to suppress rival information channels while inserting tailored messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaflets and reward-based messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Dropping leaflets offering rewards or incentives and using printed material to portray friendly forces positively and enemies negatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: leaflets offering rewards for Osama bin Laden, portraying Americans as friends, or using imagery/texts that demonize enemy leaders (e.g., picture of Mohammed Omar in crosshairs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-technology insurgent tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of simple, low-cost methods—graffiti, flyers, self-published newspapers/magazines, CDs/DVDs, and localized adverts—to spread insurgent messages and gain support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iraqi insurgents used graffiti, leaflets, cheap adverts and physical media; such tactics are cost-effective, adaptable, and can outcompete expensive official campaigns for certain audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black propaganda (false attribution and covert fronts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing material falsely attributed to hostile or neutral sources (e.g., fake radio personalities, front outlets) to disseminate pro-friendly information covertly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. employed 'Black Propaganda' by creating false radio personalities (e.g., Radio Tikrit) and paying locals/newspapers to publish American-written articles as if local. Guidance notes ethical/legal risks and the tactic’s reliance on concealed authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using truthful information channels to build credibility (e.g., Voice of America)
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing accurate, reliable information through trusted channels to exploit audiences' desire for information and thereby gain influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Voice of America' campaign is cited as successful because it offered truthful information and exploited demand for news; after censorship lifted, competition for credibility increased—shows value of truth-based messaging when credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulating domestic audiences via repetition and framing ('selling the war')
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetitive messaging and persuasive framing targeted at one's own population to justify policy or military action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation of President Bush about repeating things for 'the truth to sink in' and references to authors arguing the administration 'sold' the war; guidance: repetition, simple framing, and emotional appeals are effective for domestic persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of shocking imagery and selective coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Deploying disturbing videos/photos or curated news coverage of atrocities to influence opinions and justify actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News showed shocking images of torture and other evils under the Iraqi government; such imagery can sway public sentiment and strengthen narratives used to justify interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting children for indoctrination
rubrics_metrics.description: Designing educational materials, children's books, cartoons, and TV programs to instill ideology and normalize hostile attitudes among youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children are highly vulnerable due to developmental factors; historical examples include Nazi-era children's books and state-produced North Korean cartoons; modern example: Hamas's children's program with violent/hatred content. Guidance: use repetition, imitation, and institutional channels (schools, broadcasters) to reach children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threats, intimidation, and information control by non-state actors (e.g., drug cartels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlling the information environment through threats to journalists, public banners ('narcomantas'), pamphlets, recruitment campaigns, and cultural branding to legitimize the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mexican drug cartels use banners, pamphlets, threats to silence media, recruitment strategies, and have 'branded' 'narco' into culture via music, TV, and products. Guidance: combining fear tactics with PR/recruitment and cultural penetration increases effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: State cultural and historical framing to deflect criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Using selective historical narratives or cultural comparisons (e.g., highlighting another country’s past abuses) in state media/education to counter external criticism and justify domestic policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Chinese officials and state media use U.S. history of slavery/Native American dispossession to rebut criticism over Tibet/Xinjiang/Taiwan, framing territorial integrity as universal. Guidance: employ comparative and historical narratives to reframe critic’s moral standing.
